core: Causes of WWII: the punitive legacy of the Treaty of Versailles, the Great Depression, and the rise of fascist/militarist expansionist regimes (Nazi Germany, Fascist Italy, Imperial Japan)
The outbreak: Germany's invasion of Poland, 1 September 1939
The two sides (Allies vs Axis) and the major theaters (Europe/North Africa and the Pacific)
The Holocaust: the systematic, state-sponsored murder of six million Jews and millions of other victims, stated as documented fact
The end of the war: V-E Day (May 1945), the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki (August 1945), and Japan's surrender (V-J Day, 1945)
The total death toll (roughly 70-85 million) as the deadliest conflict in history
Aftermath: founding of the United Nations, onset of the Cold War, and decolonization
supporting: Totalitarianism and fascism as interwar political forms
Distinction between military and civilian death tolls
outOfScope: Detailed causes of World War I (named as background only)
The full history of the Cold War (named as what followed)
The full history of decolonization and imperialism (named, not owned)

claims.claim: The Treaty of Versailles (1919) imposed punitive terms on Germany (war-guilt, reparations, territorial losses, and military restrictions) that bred lasting resentment; the peace structure built around Versailles and the League of Nations unraveled in the 1930s.
The Great Depression of the 1930s caused worldwide economic collapse, mass unemployment, and poverty, which helped authoritarian and fascist movements gain power.

Fascist and militarist expansionist regimes rose in the interwar period: Nazi Germany under Hitler (chancellor 1933), Fascist Italy under Mussolini (which invaded Ethiopia in 1935), and Imperial Japan (which invaded Manchuria in 1931 and attacked China in 1937).
Britain and France pursued a policy of appeasement; the Munich Agreement (Munich Pact), signed 30 September 1938, allowed Germany to annex Czechoslovakia's Sudetenland in the hope of avoiding war.
Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, beginning World War II in Europe; Britain and France declared war in response.

The Holocaust was the systematic, state-sponsored persecution and murder of six million European Jews by Nazi Germany and its allies and collaborators; the Holocaust era spans 1933-1945, and the 'Final Solution' mass-murder phase ran from 1941 to 1945. This is documented historical fact.

Alongside six million Jews, Nazi Germany persecuted and murdered millions of other victims, including Roma, people with disabilities, Soviet prisoners of war, Polish civilians, political opponents, Jehovah's Witnesses, and gay men.
Germany surrendered unconditionally in early May 1945 (at Reims on 7 May and Berlin on 8-9 May); Victory in Europe (V-E Day) is marked on 8 May 1945.

The United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 and Nagasaki on 9 August 1945; estimates of the dead by the end of 1945 are commonly given as roughly 140,000 at Hiroshima and about 70,000-80,000 at Nagasaki, overwhelmingly civilians, with tolls rising in later years.
Japan announced its surrender on 15 August 1945 (V-J Day) and signed the formal instrument of surrender aboard the USS Missouri on 2 September 1945, ending World War II.

World War II caused roughly 70-85 million deaths and is the deadliest conflict in history; unlike most earlier wars, it killed more civilians than soldiers. The Soviet Union suffered the highest losses (about 24-27 million) and China the second highest (about 20 million).

The United Nations Charter was signed in San Francisco on 26 June 1945, and the United Nations officially came into existence on 24 October 1945 after ratification by the major powers and a majority of signatories.
The war's aftermath produced the onset of the Cold War between a U.S.-led West and a Soviet-led East, and accelerated decolonization as populations in Africa and Asia pressed for self-determination.

positions: Aggregated national tallies (e.g., National WWII Museum) give figures around 60 million once battle and civilian deaths are summed
Most modern comprehensive estimates place the total at roughly 70-85 million once war-related famine and disease are included
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the widely cited 70-85 million range as an attributed estimate and notes that figures vary substantially across sources because many deaths were never precisely recorded.

positions: Longer-term city estimates run considerably higher (e.g., Hiroshima's own estimate of about 237,000 deaths directly or indirectly over time)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson gives the by-end-of-1945 estimates as approximate, notes they rose in later years, and emphasizes the immense, overwhelmingly civilian toll without gratuitous detail.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained only generic boilerplate ('World War II is a foundational concept in History...') with no substantive historical claims; nothing in it could be verified or reused.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire boilerplate draft with researched, date-verified content.
Added the Holocaust as documented fact with USHMM attribution (six million Jews plus millions of other victims).
Attributed the 70-85 million total-death range and the atomic-bombing tolls as estimates rather than exact figures.
Corrected the loose 'UN founded April 1945 in New York' phrasing to the precise facts: Charter signed San Francisco 26 June 1945; UN came into existence 24 October 1945.
rightsIssues: All sources are REFERENCE_ONLY: authoritative for facts but not licensed for prose reuse. All lesson prose is original synthesis; no source wording was copied.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to the Holocaust
sourceRecords.provider: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum (Holocaust Encyclopedia)
sourceRecords.notes: Authoritative source for the definition of the Holocaust, the six-million figure for murdered European Jews, the 1933-1945 Holocaust era, the 1941-1945 'Final Solution' phase, and the enumeration of other victim groups (Roma, disabled people, Soviet POWs, Poles, political opponents, Jehovah's Witnesses, gay men). Read directly.

sourceRecords.title: World War II in Depth
sourceRecords.provider: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum (Holocaust Encyclopedia)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the 1 September 1939 invasion of Poland as the start of WWII in Europe and the German unconditional surrender (Reims 7 May, Berlin 9 May 1945). Read directly.

sourceRecords.title: World History, Volume 2, 13.1 An Unstable Peace
sourceRecords.notes: Supports causes of WWII: the unraveling of the Versailles/League peace, Hitler as chancellor (1933) and withdrawal from the League, Mussolini's 1935 invasion of Ethiopia, Japanese expansion (Manchuria 1931, war with China 1937), and appeasement culminating in the Munich Pact (30 September 1938). CC BY, but used REFERENCE_ONLY; prose is original. Read directly.

sourceRecords.title: World History, Volume 2, 13.4 Out of the Ashes
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the aftermath: founding of the United Nations in 1945, the onset of Cold War tensions between the U.S.-led West and Soviet-led East, and the push toward decolonization in Africa and Asia. Read directly.

sourceRecords.title: Research Starters: Worldwide Deaths of World War II
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the scale of death (tens of millions, with the museum noting worldwide estimates vary widely), the civilian-heavy toll, and the highest-loss countries (Soviet Union ~24 million+, China ~20 million). Used to anchor the widely cited 70-85 million total range as an attributed estimate. Read directly.

sourceRecords.title: Bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki - 1945
sourceRecords.provider: Atomic Heritage Foundation / National Museum of Nuclear Science & History
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the bombing dates (Hiroshima 6 August 1945, Nagasaki 9 August 1945) and death tolls (Nagasaki total ~80,000 by end of 1945; Hiroshima estimates far higher over time, including the city's own ~237,000 figure). Corroborated by Britannica/ICAN summaries via search; by-end-of-1945 figures of ~140,000 (Hiroshima) and ~70,000-80,000 (Nagasaki) are the standard estimates. Read directly.

sourceRecords.title: History of the United Nations
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the precise UN founding facts: Charter signed at the San Francisco conference (25 April-26 June 1945; signed 26 June 1945) and the UN coming into existence on 24 October 1945 after ratification. Read directly.
